report search limits instead of assuming every workflow reaches the function.

touched by the task diff or its changed data flow, inspect the task tree to
determine whether the defect persists.

do not let a focused task diff silently imply that inherited code can return
or otherwise operate successfully.

parent trees to find the code that reads the data back. Compare the writer's
and reader's resolved locations, inspect which parent directories are created,
and leave unexecuted filesystem-library behavior explicitly unestablished.

modules and package initializers that import the affected module, then state
how far an import-time failure reaches. If the explanation depends on a
language or library version fact, cite eligible documentation supplied in the
evidence catalog or state that the version fact is unestablished.

parent tree for the exact key and plausible near spellings. Inspect the task
diff and relevant consumers before describing the key's effect; do not infer
the intended spelling from the helper or variable name alone.
When a change makes a dictionary key or function argument required, search the
whole parent tree, including tests and utilities, for every builder of that
dictionary and every caller of the function. Inspect each relevant construction
site; a search limited to the implementation package cannot establish caller
compatibility.
When a documentation change describes command-line options, defaults or runtime
behavior, check every documented statement against the parser and relevant
consumers, not only statements that initially appear suspicious. Record loose
or unsupported claims and distinguish source inspection from execution.
When the commit message names a platform, product or error, search the whole
parent tree for that term before concluding that no in-scope source bears on it.
Report related occurrences without assuming they describe the same defect.

a run result supports the claim. This is an authoring-boundary candidate, not a
request to publish or mark an entry reviewed.

Label every link you draw to the task as inference and state the concrete matching basis, such as a traceback line matching a source line.

Report what their own limits, tiers or preconditions show, as source inspection. State a conclusion about the author's reason as inference, and say that the rationale is unestablished only after that inspection.

Adds or changes means the task diff registers that architecture or modifies its model or configuration class. This applies to configuration files only; read tensor headers as needed to support claims.

These are navigation hints, not established relationships; fetch bodies with web_fetch, page with evidence_index(index_id="closed_discussions"), label task links as inference with their concrete basis, and report each item’s own title and framing faithfully.

cannot establish that the change is complete.

When the task modifies, copies or closely follows a file, class or function that an earlier commit introduced,
find that commit's entry with the ancestor tools and read it before finalizing. Say which entries you read and
what they establish about the code the task relies on, including any guard, precondition or recorded defect; if
you read none, say so.

When one commit makes several edits, check whether any of them supplies a precondition another needs before
describing them as independent.

When the task starts calling an existing function, method or mechanism from a place that did not call it before,

the new call omits and state what the inspected code would do without it. If there are no other callers, say so.

When the task removes, comments out or bypasses a check, guard, conversion or initialisation, or replaces a call
that performed one, read the removed or bypassed code and say what it prevented or guaranteed. Then say whether
anything in the inspected code still prevents or guarantees it. If nothing does and the source shows an input or
call path that reaches the unguarded case, report it under findings as suspected, with its limits; do not leave
it only under uncertainty. If you could not establish a path that reaches it, say what you searched.

When the task adds or changes a model architecture, or code that names checkpoint tensors or depends on their

the changed code relies on and whether each exists with that shape, and name any stored tensors the code never
reads. Check every tensor name the code requests, including alternate and optional names, against the names in
the header, and say which are absent and which path the code then takes. Do not describe tensor layout as
unestablished while headers are available and unread.

from datasets import load_dataset
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
import math
import yaml


@disk_lru_cache("get_dataset_text")
def get_dataset_text(spec: dict):
    assert spec["dataset"] == "wiki2", "Only wiki2 implemented atm"
    dataset_text = "\n\n".join(
        load_dataset("wikitext", "wikitext-2-raw-v1", split = "test")
        ["text"]
    )
    return dataset_text


def get_test_tokens(tokenizer, rows, eval_len = 2048, eval_stride = 512):
    with ProgressBar("Tokenizing", rows) as pb:
        dataset_spec = { "dataset": "wiki2" }
        eval_tokens = tokenizer.encode(get_dataset_text(dataset_spec))
        num_tokens = eval_tokens.shape[-1]
        seqs = []
        for a in range(0, num_tokens - eval_len, eval_stride):
            b = a + eval_len
            seqs.append(eval_tokens[:, a:b])
            pb.update(len(seqs))
            if len(seqs) >= rows:
                break
    return torch.cat(seqs, dim = 0)[:, :]


@torch.inference_mode()
def main(args):

    device = torch.device(args.device)

    config_a = Config.from_directory(args.model_a)
    config_a.override_dynamic_seq_len(2048)
    tokenizer = Tokenizer.from_config(config_a)
    model_a = Model.from_config(config_a)

    model_b = Model.from_config(config_b)

    # Override tensors

            comp = yaml.safe_load(f)
        sources = {s["id"]: s["model_dir"] for s in comp["sources"]}

        collections = {}
        for o_key, o_dir in overrides.items():

            collections[o_dir].append(o_key)
        if len(collections):
            vstc = VariantSafetensorsCollection(config_a.stc)
            for o_dir, o_keys in collections.items():
                print(f" -- Overriding from: {o_dir}:")
                for o_key in o_keys:

                vstc.add_stc(o_keys, SafetensorsCollection(o_dir))
            config_a.stc = vstc

        max_diff = 0

        cos_error_sum = 0
        sqnr_sum = 0
        rows = state_a.shape[0]
        for i in range(rows):
            sa = state_a[i].to(float, copy = True)
            sb = state_b[i].to(float)
            cos_error_sum += cosine_error(sa, sb)
            sqnr_sum += sqnr(sa, sb)

            sa.abs_()
            md = ((sa.max().item()) / torch.linalg.norm(sb, 'fro').mean()).item()
            max_diff = max(max_diff, md)

        del sa, sb
        rfn_error = rfn_error_sum / rows
        cos_error = cos_error_sum / rows
        sqnr_ = sqnr_sum / rows
        print(
            f" -- {module_a.key:40}"
            f"   rfn_err: {rfn_error:.6f}"
            f"   max_diff/norm: {max_diff:.6f}"
            f"   sqnr: {sqnr_:9.6f}"

    topk_hits_count = [[0] * topk_max, [0] * topk_max]

Should complete exhaustive rankings in next couple days.\r\n\r\nBut it's good seeing a totally different evaluation criteria that uses completely separate code also identify the same exact multiplier as the best one.\r\n\r\nAnd relative to the original 3INST baseline, this multiplier produces 2.3% lower distortion which is roughly the average improvement I'm seeing in 2-bit model perplexity too. I haven't found a painless way to reliably implement LOP3 yet but it's probably a trivial patch for a smart CUDA wizard. We have any of those around here? If LOP3 isn't getting implemented in any of the EXL3 decoder kernels and it's using 2 separate [and (...) and xor(...)] instruction every pass, that's another 8-10% speedup being left on the table. Maybe this will finally make Ampere perform better?\r\n\r\n\r\nThere might also be another clever way to shave off a mov in the final re-packing steps by ordering it slightly differently as well. But do keep in mind that this is only plotting raw input <--> output for dim=1 for 8 different bitrates [1-bit - 8-bit]. However, the QTIP Trellis codes operate in 256 dimensions. So these charts are only showing 1 of the 256 distributions that effect overall performance. Also, unlike most applications where dim=1 is by far the most meaningful distribution, there's nothing special about dim=1 within a 256 dimension Trellis Coder. So it should be expected that quality of the 255 higher dimensions (aka higher-order spectral quality) actually matter equally in all dimensions for this application.\r\n\r\nJust pointing this out so we remember RMS=1.17 vs RMS=1.20 in these charts just means ~0.4% of all distributions are ~2.6% better. But that doesn't automatically mean the other 99.6% of the distribution quality will also be 2.6% better. Often higher order behavior is quite jagged and random and good distributions in one dimension only loosely correlate with distribution quality within other dimensions.\r\n\r\nThat's why I tested these six 3INST MCG values for actual MSE distortion using real 256 dimension Trellis Coding:\r\n\r\n![2-bit PLUS](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/95ea929f-b689-4abe-b8ec-35b3ee807003)\r\n\r\n![3-bit PLUS](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b522ccbe-1509-42fa-a51f-09cae88a82b9)\r\n\r\n![4-bit PLUS](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0b7445fb-0b28-463b-a499-c97bbe4eacce)\r\n\r\n\r\nY-axis re-scaled to distortion relative to an optimal codebook [2^(-2*bitrate)]\r\n\r\nAverage distortion and variance was plotted by sampling each decoder with 145-195 different 8192 [16 bit] Gaussian data chunks. This effectively simulates the precise error that occurs when quantizing and decoding 100+ of the most difficult to quantize tensors that it's possible to construct. This is the standard model (worst-case) for distortion rate calculations. It's broadly assumed that codebooks which are strongest in this worst-case setting can \"degrade gracefully\" into also being the most robust even in less-challenging settings. One of those less-challenging settings is modern LLMs weights which empirically only have ~76%-79% entropy levels (lower-bound = Llama 2; upper-bound = Llama 3). Modern LLMs haven't reached 100% entropy yet (and possibly won't/can't within the current transformer paradigm). In any case, just pointing out in passing that these codebooks I'm locating are optimized to minimize distortion in a slightly more challenging domain than what we intend to use them for here.\r\n\r\nAs for the data, my hunch that 1MAD had higher variance was right. That said, it's range still looks better by most metrics (max distortion, avg distortion, etc) than even improved 3INST decoders at 2-bit and 3-bit. However, the variance in the distortion gets worse at higher bitwidths and may become intolerable.\r\n\r\nIs there a reason 3INST was initially chosen over 1MAD? I know ik_llama.cpp also chose 3INST for their experimental IQx_KT quants so I assume there's a good reason? It's just weird because in theory I'd expect 1MAD to both run faster and provide better results on average (below 4-bits).\r\n\r\nIs it just the inconsistency (higher variance) in 1MAD quantization quality that was the problem? If that's all that's wrong, I could try to find better params for 1MAD to reduce distortion and variance some more. Default 1MAD LCG params certainly aren't optimal either. Would that make it a more attractive option again?\r\n\r\nCurrent 3INST decoder is only giving:\r\n- 2-bit quant performance equivalent to an optimal decoder with 1.87525bpw\r\n- 3-bit -- 2.86937\r\n- 4-bit -- 3.8528\r\n\r\nSUMMARY:\r\n- Using default 3INST creates ~18% more distortion (above an optimal decoder) which manifests as ~0.14bpw of wasted coding overhead at all EXL3 bitwidths.\r\n- My original proposed 3INST MCG multiplier (0xFF7A83E5) would only have ~0.12bpw coding overhead.\r\n- It's possible one of the other top 3INST MCG multipliers (like 0xCAF6A435) could bring that down to ~0.11bpw coding overhead.\r\n- If 1MAD has better params with variance more like 3INST, it could potentially have only ~0.08bpw coding overhead.     {
      "author_login": "turboderp",
      "content": "I've been holding off a little on Mistral 3.1 because I want to work out a sane way to support component models. Quantizing this way would give you Mistral 3.1 quants all over HF that won't work with the (upcoming, soon\u2122 ) multimodal features. Patching in support this way when it's \"easy\" has become a real headache in ExLlamaV2, and I'm trying to be a little more deliberate about it this time around. I'm still not sure exactly how it should look, but I plan to start architecting the multimodal support next week and I'll have a clearer picture then.\r\n\r\nAs for dynamic RoPE, it generally can't work with the current cache implementation since keys are stored after applying embeddings, so the cached keys wouldn't stay valid for a growing context. TBH I never fully understood how it's meant to work in Transformers either, since the usual caching looks like:\r\n\r\n```py\r\n        query_states = self.q_proj(hidden_states).view(hidden_shape).transpose(1, 2)\r\n        key_states = self.k_proj(hidden_states).view(hidden_shape).transpose(1, 2)\r\n        value_states = self.v_proj(hidden_states).view(hidden_shape).transpose(1, 2)\r\n\r\n        cos, sin = position_embeddings\r\n        query_states, key_states = apply_rotary_pos_emb(query_states, key_states, cos, sin)\r\n\r\n        if past_key_value is not None:\r\n            # sin and cos are specific to RoPE models; cache_position needed for the static cache\r\n            cache_kwargs = {\"sin\": sin, \"cos\": cos, \"cache_position\": cache_position}\r\n            key_states, value_states = past_key_value.update(key_states, value_states, self.layer_idx, cache_kwargs)\r\n```\r\n\r\nThen `@dynamic_rope_update` recomputes embeddings every time a token is added, but the cached keys are never updated to the new frequencies (and technically can't be without running the entire context through the forward pass, on every token.) I can see it working if keys are cached prior to embedding and RoPE is done on-the-fly, but there's a performance penalty for that, too, and support for fusing it into the attention step is patchy with both flash-attn and FlashInfer (which I'm hoping to migrate to when it supports more head dimensions.) So I've kind of been deliberately ignoring dynamic RoPE until it starts making sense to me. (:",
